name: Pramlintide
lead: Pramlintide (brand name Symlin) is a synthetic analogue of amylin, a hormone released by pancreatic beta cells together with insulin. The US FDA approved it in March 2005 as an add-on to mealtime insulin in people with type 1 or type 2 diabetes who have not reached glucose targets.[1][2] It is injected subcutaneously before meals.

For appearance, its relevance is the weight effect: amylin slows gastric emptying, promotes satiety and reduces glucagon secretion, and in trials of insulin-treated patients pramlintide lowered HbA1c modestly while body weight fell or held steady rather than rising as it typically does with insulin.[1][3][4][5] Leaner body composition is the payoff that interest in amylin-class drugs aims at, and pramlintide was an early example studied for that purpose, including in combination with metreleptin, though it is not approved for obesity.[6][7]

Its US label carries a boxed warning for severe hypoglycemia when used with insulin.[2] Newer long-acting amylin analogues such as cagrilintide, being developed by Novo Nordisk alongside semaglutide, have revived interest in the class.[13]
infobox: 37-residue peptide with proline substitutions at positions 25, 26 and 29[1][13]

paras: The labelled indication is adjunctive treatment in type 1 or type 2 diabetes in people who use mealtime insulin and have not achieved desired glucose control.[2] Wikipedia states that it can let patients use less insulin, lowers average blood sugar and blunts the sharp post-meal rise in glucose.[1] Weight loss is an observed effect in trials but not a labelled use.

Because insulin therapy commonly brings weight gain, a drug that suppresses appetite and slows digestion has drawn attention for body-weight control.[12] Obesity research has explored amylin agonism as a way to restore leptin responsiveness, and a combination of pramlintide with metreleptin produced greater weight loss than either alone in a clinical study.[6][7] Other uses described in the literature include a registered study of pramlintide for hypoglycemia after gastric bypass surgery.[14]

Pramlintide is an analogue of human amylin. Per the label, amylin is co-secreted with insulin after meals; the analogue slows gastric emptying, suppresses postprandial glucagon and increases satiety.[2][3] Amylin acts at receptors formed from the calcitonin receptor and receptor activity-modifying proteins.[3][8] A 2018 clinical study found that pramlintide, unlike liraglutide, suppressed meal-stimulated glucagon responses in type 1 diabetes, and a 1997 study found that infusing it delayed gastric emptying in men with type 1 diabetes.[15][16] Amylin's satiety effects are thought to be mediated largely through the brainstem area postrema.[13]

Pramlintide is a 37-residue peptide with a disulfide bond, sold as an acetate salt. Rat-amylin residues, including prolines, were substituted so that the analogue is less prone to forming amyloid than human amylin.[1] Wikipedia lists bioavailability of roughly 30 to 40 percent and an elimination half-life of about 48 minutes, which is why it is given around meals.[1]

The label boxed warning states that use with insulin raises the risk of severe hypoglycemia, particularly in type 1 diabetes, usually within three hours of injection, and advises insulin dose reduction and careful patient selection.[2] A randomized trial found that the amylin analogue induced migraine-like attacks in susceptible patients, a finding linked to amylin's relationship with the CGRP peptide family.[18]

Amylin was characterised in 1987 by two research groups working from islet amyloid associated with diabetes and from an insulinoma.[13] Amylin Pharmaceuticals developed the analogue, and the FDA approved Symlin on 16 March 2005; the company later became a subsidiary of AstraZeneca.[1] A randomized study with open-label extension in type 1 diabetes was published in 2002 and one-year trials in type 2 and type 1 diabetes followed in 2003 and 2004.[10][4][5]

Pramlintide is prescription-only in the US.[2] Looksmaxxing and lifting-forum discussion of it is sparse; its interest for fat loss stems from amylin-class research.[3] The popularity of GLP-1 drugs has increased attention on other satiety-hormone pathways such as amylin.[13]

One-year randomized trials of pramlintide added to insulin in type 1 and type 2 diabetes reported improvements in glycemic control with reduced or stable body weight.[4][5][9] An earlier randomized study with open-label extension in type 1 diabetes examined long-term efficacy.[10] A satisfaction study reported on treatment satisfaction in type 1 patients receiving adjunctive pramlintide.[19] Registered trials include a Phase 3 clinical-utility and safety study of 400 participants with type 1 and type 2 diabetes, a long-term safety study in 190 people with type 1 diabetes, and an observational study of 1,297 insulin users.[20][21][22]

A phase 2 exploratory study registered pharmacodynamic effects in 184 obese subjects.[11] Preclinical work found synergistic fat-specific weight loss from amylin plus leptin in rats, and a clinical study of pramlintide with metreleptin reported enhanced weight loss compared with either alone.[6][7] A systematic review lists insulin-associated weight gain as the problem such adjuncts address.[12]

card.summary: Approved amylin analogue for insulin-treated diabetes; weight loss is a side-effect signal, not an approved use.
card.note: Boxed warning for severe hypoglycemia with insulin.

quick.overview:
Pramlintide is an injectable copy of amylin, approved in 2005 as an add-on to mealtime insulin in diabetes. Trials found small improvements in blood sugar and weight loss rather than gain.

It is not approved for obesity. Obesity research on it centres on combinations such as with metreleptin.
quick.mechanism: It slows stomach emptying, reduces glucagon after meals and increases satiety.
quick.risks: The label has a boxed warning for severe hypoglycemia when used with insulin. It is prescription-only.

chain: Injected before meals as an amylin analogue
Slows stomach emptying, lowers post-meal glucagon and increases fullness
Smaller meals and less weight gain or modest weight loss in insulin-treated patients, which changes body composition
angle.text: Pramlintide copies a satiety hormone, so people on it feel full sooner and eat less, and the trials in diabetes recorded weight loss instead of gain. Its fat-loss effect has been studied mainly in diabetic patients and in obesity research combinations, not as a cosmetic drug.[3][4][6][7]
